You're evaluating Redwood alongside AWS Bedrock + Lambda-based routing and Google Vertex AI endpoints.
- Differentiators you flagged as important: low-latency fallbacks, end-to-end tracing into request metadata, and token-level cost breakdowns.

Proposed next steps:
1) Rishi will run a short comparative test plan (Redwood vs Bedrock) on your representative workload (50k small chat requests, 8k token average) to show latency distribution + token cost delta.
2) Share a short observability demo (dashboards + trace examples) and a CSV export sample of per-request cost accounting.
3) Schedule a 60-minute technical POC kickoff with your infra/ML engineer next Wed or Thu.

If that plan looks good, confirm which date/time works for the kickoff and share any additional test constraints we should include (auth patterns, VPC egress rules, or data residency requirements).

Attachments: none in this message — will include demo artifacts in Rishi's email.

- Security: we'll be evaluating SOC 2 + VPC peering for the private deployment option — can you share attestation docs?
- Observability asks: request-level traces that include model version, model variant (quantized vs fp16), and cost attribution per request. Can you show an example trace that ties a request to a particular kernel/host?

From: Rishi Malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: ACME inference platform: observability & competitive follow-up

Hi Emily — great to e-meet. Per Marissa's recap, I put together a concise test plan and included demo artifacts attached. Quick highlights below and what we'll deliver for the POC: 

Test plan (comparative):
- Workload: mirror ACME sample trace set (we'll ingest 50k requests from you or use synthetic generator with same token distribution).
- Backends: Redwood hosted (production), Redwood private (VPC, if you want), AWS Bedrock (m6i + endpoint config) — matched model family where possible.
- Metrics captured: p50/p95/p99 latency, end-to-end time, per-request token accounting, cost per 1k requests, and CPU/GPU utilization per host.
- Observability capture: full trace with spans for request ingress, routing decision, model execution (kernel selection span), kv-cache hit/miss, and response serialization. Each span will include model_version and model_variant attributes.

Deliverables before kickoff: 
1) redwood-observability-demo.pdf (attached) — screenshots of the console, a sample trace, and how to filter by model_variant.
2) redwood-performance-results.csv (attached) — sample CSV from an internal comparison run showing latency percentiles and per-request token cost breakdown.
3) Access to a demo dashboard: https://app.redwood.ai/demo/dashboard/acme (link included below).

Notes on the competitive angle:
- Hyperscalers can give broad coverage, but their per-request cost accounting is typically coarse (endpoint-level) and lacks token-level transparency. Redwood provides token-level cost attribution and built-in fallbacks that let you route to a cheaper quantized variant for non-critical requests — we can show exact cost delta during the POC.
- For latency, we instrument kernel selection and show the p99 impact of cold KV-cache misses; those traces usually identify whether slowdowns are execution or I/O-bound.

Attachments included: redwood-observability-demo.pdf, redwood-performance-results.csv

Let me know if you want us to run the initial synthetic comparison before the kickoff; otherwise we'll do the baseline during the POC week and share results within 48 hours.

Cheers,
Rishi Malhotra
Solutions Engineer
